statement: In people who used cannabis frequently, the evidence is insufficient to say whether differences in memory and thinking tests remain after they have stopped for days or weeks, and the question is disputed. Differences were smaller in studies that required longer abstinence: in a meta-analysis of cross-sectional studies of adolescents and young adults (Scott et al., 2018; AMSTAR 2 confidence critically low), the 15 studies that required more than 72 hours without cannabis before testing (928 participants; 7 to 90 days by the first reader's reading of the Table) found an average difference from comparison groups with minimal use of −0.08 standard deviations (95% CI −0.22 to 0.07), against −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22) in the 54 studies that required 72 hours or less or did not say (P = .01; the authors say the abstinence associations hold only at thresholds not corrected for multiple comparisons). This compares different studies, not the same people before and after stopping; the interval includes no difference and reaches −0.22, close to the overall difference of −0.25; only 14 of the 69 studies reported checking abstinence; at least 7 of the 15 longer-abstinence studies come from papers sharing one author, and 11 of the 15 had age ranges ending at 20 or younger. A systematic review of 2004-2015 studies (Broyd et al., 2016; critically low) found eighteen studies of people abstinent for more than a day, most often 21 to 35 days and few for longer: some found poorer attention, verbal or working memory or psychomotor speed after 23 to 53 days of abstinence, or poorer executive function in older adults abstinent more than 28 days, while others found no difference from controls, including a prospective study in which adolescents who had stopped did not differ from controls and a cohort in which people who had stopped heavy use for at least 12 months did not differ on any test from people who had not used. It rated persistence as mixed for verbal learning and memory, working memory, attention and planning-type executive functions, called recovery contentious and suggested that verbal learning and memory may recover with prolonged abstinence, while its summary table is firmer than these ratings (likely persistent effects on attention and psychomotor function, possible ones on verbal learning and memory). A narrative review of the same year (Curran et al., 2016) states that studies converge on no impairment beyond 4–6 weeks, citing two earlier sources, and adds that brain cannabinoid receptor levels return to normal after about 4 weeks of monitored abstinence, which is not a test of memory or thinking. In a New Zealand birth cohort, people with dependence at 2 or more of 5 interviews whose at least weekly use began before 18, and who used cannabis weekly or less in the year before testing at 38, had lower IQ at 38 than in childhood (17 people, p = .03 by a test the paper does not describe), but they had used on up to 52 days that year and were not compared with people who never used, so this is not a test of abstinence (Meier et al., 2012). The individual abstinence studies are known here only through the reviews' descriptions, and the reviews share studies. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: It is not clear. In studies that asked people to go more than 3 days without cannabis before the test, the average gap in scores was small and could be zero, though a gap nearly as big as the average across all studies is not ruled out; and these were different studies, not the same people before and after stopping. Studies of people who had stopped for about 3 to 8 weeks disagree: some found lower scores on some tests, others found none. Few studies followed people for longer; in one, people who had stopped heavy use for a year or more did not differ on any test from people who had not used. Reviews read this evidence in opposite ways.
population: People who used cannabis frequently or heavily, mostly adolescents and young adults (a few studies of older adults), tested after a period without cannabis
exposure: Stopping cannabis for more than 72 hours to about 3 months before testing (mostly 3 to 5 weeks; abstinence checked in a minority of studies), and in a few cohorts for 12 months or more
comparator: People who used little or no cannabis; people who continued using; or the same people tested before they stopped (prospective studies)
outcome: Memory, attention, processing-speed, psychomotor and executive test scores after abstinence, and in one cohort full-scale IQ
magnitude: Scott et al. 2018 (raw-score d against comparison groups): required abstinence more than 72 h −0.08 (95% CI −0.22 to 0.07; 15 studies, n = 928, P = .29) against 72 h or less −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22; 54 studies, n = 7,799); chi-square 6.36, P = .01 (abstinence associations described by the authors as holding at uncorrected thresholds); longer mean reported abstinence went with smaller differences (beta 0.059, P = .04 uncorrected; 28 studies); required abstinence mean 152.7 h (SD 335.2), none or unstated in 22 studies, 1 to 72 h in 32, more than 72 h in 15; monitored in 14. Broyd et al. 2016: eighteen abstinence studies (eleven cross-sectional, abstinent 7 days to more than 1 year; seven prospective, 21 days to 4–8 years); persistence rated +– for verbal learning and memory (9 studies), working memory (7), attention (10), planning-type executive functions (9) and verbal fluency (4), + for psychomotor function (6), – for other memory functions, time estimation and decision making. Meier et al. 2012: dependence at 2 or more waves, at least weekly use before 18, and weekly or less use in the year before testing (median 14 days, range 0 to 52; n = 17), childhood to adult IQ about 102 to 97.5, p = .03 (values read from a figure).

evidence.locator: Abstract (AM p. 2); Figure 1, PRISMA flow diagram (AM p. 27)
evidence.extracted: Systematic review of studies published January 2004 to February 2015 on acute and chronic effects of cannabis and cannabinoids on cognitive task performance and on persistence or recovery after abstinence: 3,021 records from PubMed and 3,220 from Scopus, 356 full-text records screened, 260 excluded and 105 studies included in a qualitative synthesis, with nothing pooled (editors' arithmetic on the study card: 356 minus 260 leaves 96, so the flow does not add up).

evidence.locator: Discussion › Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Recovery after prolonged abstinence is called contentious. Eighteen studies examined persistence or recovery after more than 24 hours of abstinence, most often for several weeks (21–35 days), only a few for longer: eleven cross-sectional comparisons of people who had stopped (abstinent 7 days to more than 1 year) with people still using and/or controls, 9 of them in adolescents or young adults; and seven prospective studies that tested people at baseline and follow-up over 21 days to 4–8 years of abstinence, 2 of them confounded by concurrent drug treatment (refs 63, 93).

evidence.locator: Discussion › Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Cross-sectional studies: some aspects of attention, verbal and working memory and psychomotor speed remained impaired in adolescents abstinent 28 days (ref. 65) and 35 days (ref. 67), while other aspects and domains did not; poorer performance went with lifetime use (ref. 65) or earlier onset in 30-day abstinent adolescents, and predicted relapse within a year (ref. 95); adolescents abstinent 53 days showed impaired working memory and risk taking (ref. 85); young adults abstinent up to 4 weeks had poorer verbal fluency than controls (ref. 119); older adults abstinent more than 28 days were impaired on executive function and information processing but not on attention or working memory (ref. 57). In identical twins discordant for use, with more than 12 months' abstinence, the twins who had used did worse on Block Design, with trends on delayed and cued recall and finger tapping; that study's authors read it as evidence against long-term effects (ref. 64).

evidence.locator: Discussion › Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Of the prospective studies, only two controlled for ability before use: in one, adolescents who had stopped did not differ from controls on any cognitive measure (ref. 79); in the other (ref. 60, Dunedin), use before 18 was followed by greater IQ decline by 38 that persisted after stopping or cutting down in the past year. Poor verbal learning improved in adolescents by 2 weeks of abstinence, while visual search remained impaired at 3 weeks relative to baseline (ref. 55); adults improved on critical tracking and divided attention over 8–23 days of abstinence but remained impaired against controls (ref. 91); in a cohort assessed three times, 4 years apart, people who had stopped heavy use for at least 12 months improved relative to people who continued heavy use on immediate verbal memory and did not differ from people who had not used on any cognitive measure (ref. 66).

evidence.locator: Discussion › Persistence or recovery of function with abstinence, 4th paragraph (begins AM p. 10, continues on p. 11)
evidence.extracted: The authors' reading: consistent with earlier findings (refs 134, 135), some but not all recent studies suggest that impaired verbal learning and memory may recover with prolonged abstinence, yet evidence for persistent cognitive dysfunction continues to emerge; an earlier study using sensitive measures of brain function found attentional processing deficits related to duration of exposure in people abstinent 2 years (ref. 141); well-controlled prospective studies from current use through prolonged abstinence are called for.

People abstinent twenty-three days remained impaired against controls on sustained and divided attention despite improving with longer abstinence (ref. 91), with poorer attention linked to younger age of onset in that study and in 30-day abstinent adolescents (ref. 95); other studies found no difference between people abstinent after past use and controls on broader attention measures (refs 57, 63, 64, 79, 95). The authors suggest that attentional impairment may reflect residual effects that fade gradually as cannabinoids are cleared from the body.

evidence.locator: Table 1, Persistence with abstinence column and Number of studies ABSTINENCE column (AM pp. 24-25); Table 2, Recovery of function with abstinence (AM p. 26)
evidence.extracted: The review's ratings of the evidence for impairment persisting with abstinence (number of abstinence studies): verbal learning and memory +– (9); working memory +– (7); attention +– (10); psychomotor function + (6); planning, reasoning, interference control and problem solving +– (9); verbal fluency +– (4); other memory functions – (4); time estimation – (1); decision making – (3); attentional bias and inhibition not investigated. Key: + weak, based on few studies; +– mixed; – little or no evidence; the ratings are the authors' subjective consensus. Table 2 summarises recovery with abstinence more firmly than Table 1, as likely persistent effects on attention and psychomotor function, possible persistent effects on verbal learning and memory, and insufficient and mixed evidence.

evidence.locator: Long-term effects, 1st paragraph (begins p. 296, continues on p. 297) and 2nd paragraph (p. 297)
evidence.extracted: Second-hand (narrative review): case-control studies of non-acute effects are called inconsistent; the most consistent finding is poorer encoding of new episodic memories, with persisting deficits in some studies over the first few days of abstinence but little evidence of deficits at 28 days (as summarised from a review, ref. 25); long-term memory impairments have been reported mainly in frequent, heavy use, and confounders make cause and effect hard to establish.

evidence.locator: Effects persisting after stopping use, paragraph (p. 298); reference list, refs 58 and 59 (p. 304)
evidence.extracted: Second-hand: the review states that studies of long-term effects after stopping show no cognitive impairment persisting beyond 4–6 weeks of abstinence, citing two sources (ref. 58, Pope and colleagues, 2001, a study of people with long-term use; ref. 59, Schreiner and Dunn, 2012, a meta-analysis of residual effects after prolonged abstinence). As further support it cites PET imaging in which reduced cortical cannabinoid (CB1) receptor availability in people who used cannabis chronically, correlated with years of use, returned to control levels after about 4 weeks of continuously monitored abstinence (ref. 30), and after as little as 2 days in one study (ref. 31); receptor availability is not a test of memory or thinking. Imaging studies of persisting effects are called cross-sectional, with different abstinence intervals and confounds, and longitudinal studies are called for.
evidence.quote: converging to show that cognitive impairments do not persist beyond 4–6 weeks after abstinence

evidence.locator: Results › What Is the Effect of Cessation of Cannabis Use?, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 and its legend
evidence.extracted: Among people dependent at 2 or more of the 5 assessments, split by weekly use before 18 and by frequency of use in the year before testing at 38: adolescent onset with infrequent use (weekly or less; median 14 days, range 0 to 52; n = 17), childhood to adult IQ about 102 to 97.5, p = .03; adolescent onset with frequent use (median 365 days; n = 19) about 97 to 89, p = .0002; adult onset with infrequent use (n = 13) p = .73; adult onset with frequent use (n = 20) p = .11 (IQ values read approximately from the figure by the first reader). The p values compare each group's own childhood and adult IQ; no comparison with the group that never used is reported, and the infrequent group includes people who used on up to 52 days that year, so it is not an abstinent group.

risk_of_bias.note: The abstinence contrast is between studies that also differ in laboratory, sample and protocol (at least 7 of the 15 longer-abstinence studies from papers sharing one author; rows that apparently share a comparison group fall in opposite subgroups); abstinence was checked in 14 of 69 studies; the abstinence studies in the systematic review are mostly small and cross-sectional, and the prospective ones mostly lack retested comparison groups, so practice is not separated from recovery (AMSTAR 2 critically low: cards sc_scott_2018, sc_broyd_2016).

inconsistency.note: Studies disagree, some finding differences after 23 to 53 days and others none after 12 months or more, and the two reviews of the same years read them in opposite ways; length of abstinence alone does not explain the disagreement.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: the individual abstinence studies are known only through the reviews' descriptions, some with misplaced citations (card sc_broyd_2016, reporting issues), and the narrative review's statement rests on two sources not read and on receptor imaging rather than tests; abstinence mostly lasted 3 to 5 weeks.

imprecision.note: The longer-abstinence estimate rests on 15 small studies (928 participants), and its interval (−0.22 to 0.07) includes no difference and reaches −0.22, close to the overall difference (−0.25); the between-study test (P = .01) is not corrected for the several study features tested.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed for the abstinence subgroup or the abstinence studies; not rated down separately.

large_effect.note: Not applicable to a claim of insufficient evidence.

dose_response.note: Longer mean reported abstinence went with smaller differences across 28 studies (P = .04, uncorrected), a between-study gradient that may reflect other study differences; no upgrade.

plausible_confounding.note: People who manage to stop may differ from those who continue, in either direction; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low and is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision: very low. Worded as insufficient evidence: differences are smaller after longer abstinence in a between-study comparison, but neither their disappearance nor their persistence after weeks can be shown with precision. Overlap: the abstinence studies in the systematic review and the longer-abstinence studies in the meta-analysis share studies (Fried et al., 2005, for example, is in both), and the narrative review adds no new data, so the sources are not independent replication. Status contested: credible studies point both ways, and two reviews of the same years draw opposite conclusions (one calls recovery contentious, the other says studies converge on no impairment beyond 4–6 weeks).

debate.question: After people who used cannabis often stop, do differences in memory and thinking go away within days or weeks, or do some remain?
debate.evidence_yes: The systematic review that describes the abstinence studies one by one (Broyd et al., 2016; sc_broyd_2016; funded by the Australian Research Council and the National Health and Medical Research Council; no conflicts declared) reports deficits after weeks without cannabis in several of them: some aspects of attention, verbal and working memory and psychomotor speed in adolescents abstinent 28 and 35 days; working memory and risk taking in adolescents abstinent 53 days; poorer verbal fluency in young adults abstinent up to 4 weeks; executive function and information processing in older adults abstinent more than 28 days; adults who improved on tracking and divided attention over 8 to 23 days but stayed below controls; visual search still impaired after 3 weeks in adolescents whose verbal learning had improved; and, in identical twins of whom one had used and had been abstinent more than 12 months, poorer Block Design with trends on delayed recall and finger tapping. Poorer performance after abstinence went with more lifetime use or earlier onset in two adolescent studies and predicted relapse within a year in one. Its authors conclude that evidence for persistent dysfunction continues to emerge, and cite an earlier study that used sensitive measures of brain function and found attention-processing deficits related to years of use in people abstinent 2 years. In the meta-analysis that found smaller differences after longer abstinence (Scott et al., 2018; sc_scott_2018), the interval for studies requiring more than 72 hours (−0.22 to 0.07) reaches −0.22, close to the overall difference of −0.25, so a difference of nearly that size is not ruled out. In the Dunedin cohort, people with dependence at 2 or more interviews whose at least weekly use began before 18, and who used weekly or less in the year before testing, still had lower IQ than in childhood (17 people, p = .03), which its authors read as incomplete recovery, although these people were not abstinent (Meier et al., 2012; sc_meier_2012).
debate.evidence_no: In a meta-analysis of 69 cross-sectional samples of young people (Scott et al., 2018; sc_scott_2018; funded by the US Department of Veterans Affairs, with no role for the funder; one author reports royalties from the Brain Resource Center), studies that required more than 72 hours without cannabis found an average difference of −0.08 (−0.22 to 0.07), against −0.30 in studies requiring 72 hours or less (P = .01, at thresholds the authors describe as not corrected for multiple comparisons), and longer mean reported abstinence went with smaller differences (P = .04, uncorrected); the zero or unknown abstinence studies did not drive the contrast, as the authors report, and they read it as residual effects of recent use or withdrawal rather than lasting change. In the systematic review that lists persisting deficits, the two prospective studies that controlled for ability before use include one in which adolescents who had stopped did not differ from controls on any measure, and in a cohort tested three times 4 years apart, people who had stopped heavy use for at least 12 months improved relative to people who continued on immediate verbal memory and did not differ from people who had not used on any test; several studies found no difference on broader attention measures between people who had stopped and controls, and verbal learning improved by 2 weeks in adolescents (Broyd et al., 2016; sc_broyd_2016). Its authors suggest that attention deficits may be residual effects that fade as cannabinoids are cleared, and that verbal learning and memory may recover with prolonged abstinence. A narrative review (Curran et al., 2016; sc_curran_2016; funded by the US National Institutes of Health and the UK Medical Research Council; competing interests declared, with details only in the web version) states that studies are converging on no impairment beyond 4–6 weeks, citing a study of people with long-term use and a meta-analysis of residual effects, and adds that brain cannabinoid receptor levels return to normal after about 4 weeks of monitored abstinence.
debate.neither_can_show: Most abstinence studies compare different people once, and people who manage to stop may differ from people who continue in ability, motivation or other drug use; apart from two prospective studies, none of the studies in these reviews tested people before they first used. Where the same people are retested without a retested comparison group, improvement from practice cannot be separated from recovery. Only 14 of the 69 studies in the meta-analysis reported checking abstinence, most abstinence periods were 3 to 5 weeks, and few studies went beyond a year. The between-study abstinence contrast is also a contrast of laboratories and samples: at least 7 of the 15 longer-abstinence studies come from papers sharing one author, and 11 have age ranges ending at 20 or younger. A difference that remains after stopping need not have been caused by cannabis, and receptor imaging does not measure memory or thinking. Differences between group averages are not the same as problems in daily life. The individual abstinence studies, and the two sources behind the 4–6 weeks statement, are known here only through the reviews' descriptions.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). Part of the small difference seen in people who use cannabis often is probably the after-effect of recent use: the difference is smaller in studies that required more than a few days without cannabis, and attention and verbal learning improved over days to weeks in the studies that retested people. Whether a small difference remains after several weeks is open: the reports of persisting deficits come from small cross-sectional samples, mostly of adolescents, and the reports of no difference from a between-study comparison and a few cohorts, all known here through reviews. For a year or more without cannabis, the evidence is a handful of studies with mixed results. The statement that impairment does not persist beyond 4–6 weeks is firmer than the evidence these reviews describe, and so is the statement that impairment clearly persists.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Studies that test the same people before they start using, while they use and repeatedly after they stop, with urine tests confirming abstinence at each visit, beside comparison groups retested on the same schedule to allow for practice; follow-up from days to years; enough people to analyse results by length of verified abstinence; and a pre-registered meta-analysis of individual participants' data stratified by verified abstinence. None of the sources read reports such a study.
